citation: Villanueva C, Colomo A, Bosch A, Concepción M, Hernandez-Gea V, Aracil C, Graupera I, Poca M, Alvarez-Urturi C, Gordillo J, Guarner-Argente C, Santaló M, Muñiz E, Guarner C. Transfusion strategies for acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding. N Engl J Med. 2013;368(1):11-21
one_liner: In severe acute UGIB, a restrictive transfusion strategy (Hb <7 g/dL) reduced 45-day mortality (5% vs 9%) and further bleeding (10% vs 16%) compared to a liberal strategy (Hb <9 g/dL).

pico.population: Adults with severe acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding (haematemesis, melena, or both) requiring hospitalisation and urgent endoscopy.
pico.intervention: Restrictive red-cell transfusion strategy: transfuse when Hb <7 g/dL, target 7–9 g/dL.
pico.comparison: Liberal strategy: transfuse when Hb <9 g/dL, target 9–11 g/dL.
pico.outcome: Primary: all-cause mortality within 45 days. Key secondary: further bleeding, adverse events, transfusion reactions, length of stay.

background.existing_knowledge: Red-cell transfusion is common in acute UGIB, but optimal haemoglobin thresholds were uncertain; extrapolation from critical care restrictive trials was limited because acute GI bleeding populations were excluded, and there were mechanistic concerns that transfusion might worsen portal pressure and rebleeding in portal-hypertensive haemorrhage.
background.knowledge_gap: Whether a restrictive transfusion strategy improves outcomes compared with a liberal strategy in severe acute UGIB.
background.hypothesis: Restrictive transfusion (Hb <7 g/dL) would reduce mortality and rebleeding compared to liberal (Hb <9 g/dL).

methods.design: Randomised, single-centre, pragmatic, open-label trial with concealed allocation, stratified by cirrhosis, intention-to-treat analysis.
methods.setting: Hospital de la Santa Creu i Sant Pau, Barcelona; enrolled June 2003–December 2009.

inclusion: Adults (>18 years) with haematemesis (or bloody nasogastric aspirate), melaena, or both, confirmed by staff
exclusion: Low-risk presentation (clinical Rockall score 0 with Hb ≥12 g/dL)

methods.intervention: Restrictive transfusion strategy: transfuse packed red cells when Hb <7 g/dL; post-transfusion target 7–9 g/dL; 1 unit at a time with reassessment.
methods.comparison: Liberal transfusion strategy: transfuse when Hb <9 g/dL; post-transfusion target 9–11 g/dL; 1 unit at a time with reassessment; both arms permitted off-protocol transfusion for anaemia symptoms/signs, massive bleeding, or surgery.
methods.blinding: Open-label (strategy-based transfusion; blinding not feasible); primary endpoint objective (all-cause mortality).
methods.sample_size_power: 430 patients/group (860 total) required to detect ≥5% absolute mortality difference (assumed 10% mortality in liberal arm) with two-sided α=0.05 and β=0.20 (80% power).
secondary_outcomes: Further bleeding (haemodynamic instability or Hb drop ≥2 g/dL within 6 hours)
methods.follow_up: 45 days (primary endpoint); survival presented to 6 weeks.

headline_bullets: Restrictive strategy reduced 45-day mortality: 5% vs 9% (HR 0.55, 95% CI 0.33–0.92, P=0.02)
Further bleeding lower with restrictive: 10% vs 16% (HR 0.62, 95% CI 0.43–0.91, P=0.01)
Marked reduction in blood exposure: mean 1.5 vs 3.7 units; 51% vs 14% received no transfusion
Fewer adverse events and transfusion reactions in restrictive arm
In variceal bleeding, liberal transfusion increased portal pressure gradient (P=0.03), while restrictive did not

outcomes_table.outcome: Death from any cause within 45 days

outcomes_table.note: Definition: haemodynamic instability or Hb drop ≥2 g/dL within 6 hours

safety: Cardiac complications: 11% vs 16% (HR 0.64, P=0.04); myocardial infarction: 0 vs 8 (2%)
Restrictive strategy had fewer overall complications and transfusion-related harms.

domains.notes: Computer-generated random numbers; sealed, consecutively numbered, opaque envelopes; stratified by cirrhosis; blocks of four. Allocation concealed.

Open-label; could influence co-interventions and thresholds for declaring further bleeding or complications; mitigated by standardised definitions and objective primary endpoint (all-cause mortality).
921 randomised; 32 withdrawn after randomisation; ITT analysis included 444 restrictive and 445 liberal. Major protocol violation more common in restrictive arm (9% vs 3%, P<0.001) but <10%.
Protocol violations higher in restrictive arm but still low; analyses were ITT.
Groups similar at baseline (mean complete Rockall 5.3 vs 5.4; shock at admission 28% vs 31%).
Rapid enrolment and endoscopy: randomisation ~19 vs 18 min from admission; gastroscopy ~5 vs 5 hours.
Clear Hb exposure difference: lowest Hb 7.3 vs 8.0 g/dL; discharge Hb 9.2 vs 10.1; RBC units 1.5 vs 3.7 (all P<0.001).
Protocolised acute management: emergency endoscopy within 6 hours; high-dose IV omeprazole for peptic ulcer; vasoactive therapy and antibiotics for portal hypertension; rescue pathways specified.

Time-to-event methods with prespecified Cox adjustment factors (mortality model adjusted for age, in-hospital bleeding, cirrhosis, Rockall score; further bleeding model included shock and baseline Hb).

internal_validity.verdict: Moderate-to-strong: allocation concealment and objective primary endpoint support causal inference, with the main limitation being open-label delivery and higher (though <10%) protocol deviations in the restrictive arm.

domains.notes: Adults with severe UGIB (median-to-high Rockall; 31% cirrhosis; 49% peptic ulcer; 21% oesophageal varices) managed in a specialist bleeding unit with rapid access to endoscopy and portal pressure measurements in a subset.

Benefits likely depend on timely endoscopic and pharmacological haemostasis and availability of rescue interventions; applicability may be attenuated where such pathways are delayed or unavailable. Excluded exsanguinating bleeding, recent ACS/stroke/TIA, low-risk presentations, and prior recent transfusion.

external_validity.verdict: Highly generalisable to hospitalised, non-exsanguinating UGIB managed with modern haemostatic pathways; limited for massive haemorrhage and patients with very recent major ischaemic events.

strengths: Concealed allocation with stratification for cirrhosis
Clinically meaningful separation in haemoglobin and transfusion exposure
Mechanistic portal-pressure substudy consistent with clinical outcomes
limitations: Post-randomisation withdrawals (32) and more protocol violations in restrictive arm (9% vs 3%)
Exclusions limit applicability to exsanguinating bleeding and very recent high-risk cardiovascular events
Some secondary outcomes could be influenced by care decisions in an unblinded trial

critical_appraisal.summary: Well-conducted RCT with concealed allocation and objective primary outcome, demonstrating mortality benefit with restrictive transfusion; open-label design and single-centre setting are limitations, but results are consistent with mechanistic data and subsequent meta-analyses.
strengths: Clinically meaningful separation in transfusion exposure
weaknesses: Higher protocol deviations in restrictive arm

sections.authors_conclusion: Restrictive transfusion strategy (Hb <7 g/dL) improved survival and reduced rebleeding and transfusion-related harms in severe UGIB, supporting its use as standard of care.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Restrictive transfusion (Hb <7 g/dL) should be standard for hospitalised UGIB without exsanguinating haemorrhage or recent major cardiovascular events.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Patients with severe UGIB (haematemesis, melena) managed with urgent endoscopy and haemostatic therapies.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Not applicable to exsanguinating haemorrhage or patients with very recent ACS/stroke.
implementation_caveats: Requires rapid endoscopy and haemostatic control
Consider higher threshold (e.g., 8 g/dL) in patients with cardiovascular disease per guidelines

controversies.notes: Concerns that open-label management could influence rebleeding/rescue decisions and complication ascertainment were raised in published correspondence, although mortality (primary outcome) is less susceptible to bias.

Exclusion of very recent acute coronary syndrome/stroke/TIA and limited data in high-risk ischaemic subgroups meant the one-size-fits-all Hb <7 threshold remained debated, driving guideline nuance (e.g., higher thresholds in known cardiovascular disease).

Benefit was clear in Child–Pugh A/B cirrhosis but not in Child–Pugh C (HR 1.04; wide CI), raising questions about competing risks and whether transfusion strategy meaningfully alters outcomes in advanced liver failure.

The TRIGGER cluster-randomised feasibility trial demonstrated that implementing hospital-level transfusion policies in UGIB is feasible but highlighted practice variability and the need for adequately powered effectiveness trials.
A large systematic review/meta-analysis of RCTs (including re-analysed cluster data) found restrictive strategies reduced mortality and rebleeding overall, with no clear increase in ischaemic events.

Contemporary UGIB guidance widely endorses restrictive RBC transfusion around Hb ≤7 g/dL in patients without cardiovascular disease, with more liberal thresholds (~8 g/dL) when cardiovascular disease is present.

context_related_trials.relation: Cluster-randomised feasibility trial demonstrating that implementing hospital-level restrictive transfusion policies in UGIB is feasible but highlighted practice variability and the need for adequately powered effectiveness trials.

unresolved_questions: Optimal transfusion threshold in patients with cardiovascular disease
Benefit in Child-Pugh C cirrhosis unclear
Need for larger multicentre trials to confirm effectiveness across diverse settings

numbers_to_remember: 51% received no transfusion in restrictive arm
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: In severe UGIB, transfuse only when Hb <7 g/dL (target 7-9) to reduce mortality, rebleeding, and transfusion complications.
